Voskhod 1. The Soviet Union launched the first spacecraft to carry a multi-person crew on October 12, 1964. Voskhod 1 carried three cosmonauts—Vladimir Komarov, Boris Yegorov, and Konstantin Feoktistov—in a cramped cabin with no spacesuits. The three crew members flew without spacesuits because they were unable to separate; the capsule was simply too small, and they relied on the cabin's atmosphere for survival.

Feoktistov was not a traditional cosmonaut but a spacecraft designer—a political move to show Soviet civilian involvement in space. The mission was essentially a hastily redesigned Vostok capsule, modified to carry additional crew members in this rapid Soviet response to American advances in the Space Race.

Five months later came Voskhod 2, launched on March 18, 1965, which achieved the first spacewalk. Alexei Leonov exited the spacecraft, tethered to the cabin. His spacewalk lasted about 12 minutes, and during that time something unexpected happened: his suit inflated in the vacuum, expanding beyond its normal shape. Leonov had to reduce air pressure inside the suit to re-enter the airlock. Both Voskhod missions were rapid Soviet responses to American achievements, competing intensely for firsts in what had become the defining competition of the Space Age.
